prize_parts.citation: for developing targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases to destroy chosen proteins

statement.case_for: Induced-proximity degradation passes my own test of being a game-changer: it is a simple chemical idea (a small molecule that brings a target and an E3 ligase together) that opened a new class of drug mechanism and made previously undruggable proteins reachable. It has already had real consequences: it is a standard chemical-biology tool for acute protein depletion, and many degraders are in clinical trials. Crews and Deshaies founded the PROTAC concept and Handa identified cereblon as the thalidomide target, which explains molecular glue degraders. That gives a prize covering both the heterobifunctional and the glue branches within the three-person limit. It has the broadest support in the opening round (five members ranked it, including a first place from the chair and top-three placements from Chabes, Aili and me), so it is the most plausible place for the committee to converge.
statement.case_against: Allocation is genuinely contested and there is no approved degrader drug yet. Ciulli (VHL ligands, ternary-complex structure), Sakamoto, Ito, Gray and others have real claims, so any trio leaves out serious contributors. Recognition could be premature if the clinical record disappoints. My own first choice, Car-Parrinello, is cleaner on attribution and maturity but has almost no support, and I should not mistake my own field loyalty for committee consensus.

responses.point: Linke ranks B027 first and would credit Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, treating the cereblon/glue branch as a separate discovery that would crowd the citation.
responses.response: I agree on the ranking but not on dropping Handa. The VHL-based PROTAC work is a refinement of a concept Crews and Deshaies had already established, whereas Handa's identification of cereblon is an independent mechanistic discovery that explains an old drug and underpins the glue branch. A citation about degradation by E3 recruitment should cover both branches. Ciulli is the strongest fourth name, and I accept that the choice is a close, contestable priority judgement.

responses.point: Chabes ranks base editing first and argues that a single-laureate prize for David R. Liu is the cleanest configuration, with Target-AID as a parallel but secondary route.
responses.response: I share this view of the attribution and ranked B038 second for the same reason. A one-person prize is attractive, but I would not make it first yet. The clinical record for base editors is short, and the 2020 CRISPR prize makes the committee's framing question harder. Base editing is a strong fallback if the degradation allocation cannot be settled, but I do not think it is more mature than degraders.

responses.point: Sparr ranks lipid nanoparticles first (Cullis, Madden, Hope) and phase separation second, treating them as chemistry concepts with proven or growing consequences.
responses.response: The medical consequences of lipid nanoparticles are not in doubt, but I am not persuaded they are a chemistry game-changer of the kind this prize rewards, since much of the contribution is formulation and the allocation among six credited names is very unstable. Anderson, Langer and MacLachlan have claims that Cullis, Madden and Hope would exclude, and the 2023 Medicine prize overlaps. On condensates I side with Brzezinski's maturity concern: it is still unclear which condensates are truly liquid and functional in cells.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks long-range protein electron transfer (Gray, Winkler) first and nitrogenase second, emphasising time-resolved physical mechanism and attribution that fits two or three names.
responses.response: I find the Gray-Winkler attribution the cleanest on the shortlist and agree it is a mature, quantitative result that connects theory and experiment, which is what I want. My reservation is how new it is as a prize story, because the Marcus theory has already been recognised. I would put it ahead of nitrogenase, whose mechanism is still debated, as you note yourself. I would keep it as a serious candidate for later rounds.

uncertainties: Whether Handa or Ciulli is the better third name beside Crews and Deshaies, and whether Sakamoto's early PROTAC paper changes the priority picture.
Whether the committee views the absence of an approved degrader as too early.
Whether Car-Parrinello can attract any support beyond me and the chair's last-place ranking.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My Warshel/Uppsala connections concern simulation and ribosome work, and I have no stated link to Car, Parrinello, Crews, Deshaies, Handa or other credited names.
